nameStory: This dragonfly earns its "clubtail" name from the distinctive club-shaped widening at the tip of its abdomen, like a tiny baseball bat. The "least" part refers to its status as one of the smaller clubtail species, while "eastern" indicates its range primarily in the eastern United States and Appalachian regions.
description: The Eastern Least Clubtail is a medium-sized dragonfly with the characteristic clubbed abdomen tip that gives its family their common name. Like all dragonflies, it has four large, transparent wings that it holds perpendicular to its body when at rest, and large compound eyes for spotting prey. These agile hunters patrol waterways and nearby areas, catching mosquitoes, flies, and other small insects on the wing. Adults typically measure around 2-3 inches in length with a wingspan of about 3-4 inches.

idTips.label: Clubbed abdomen tip
idTips.description: The abdomen widens noticeably at the very end, creating a club or paddle shape that's easily visible even from a distance

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are transparent with fine black veining, lacking the colored patches seen in some other dragonfly families

idTips.label: Separated eyes
idTips.description: Unlike darners, the large compound eyes don't touch at the top of the head but remain distinctly separated

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often rests on bare ground, rocks, or low vegetation with wings held straight out from the body

idTips.label: Yellow and black markings
idTips.description: Body typically shows a pattern of yellow stripes and spots against a darker background, though colors may vary

habitat: Look for Eastern Least Clubtails near clean streams, small rivers, and spring-fed waterways, especially in wooded areas of the Appalachian regions and eastern New England. They prefer areas with rocky or sandy bottoms and good water quality, as their aquatic nymphs are sensitive to pollution. Adults can often be spotted perching on streamside rocks, bare soil, or low vegetation in sunny openings.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their aquatic nymph stage in late spring, with peak emergence typically in May and early June when water temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Prime time for spotting adults patrolling territories and mating near suitable waterways. Look for them perched on rocks or hunting from low perches during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down as temperatures drop. Eggs laid earlier in the season develop into nymphs that will spend the winter underwater.
seasonality.winter: Only the aquatic nymph stage survives winter, living on stream bottoms and growing slowly in the cold water until ready to emerge as adults the following spring.

funFact: Eastern Least Clubtail nymphs are underwater ninjas — they can shoot out their extendable lower jaw like a harpoon to snatch prey, extending it up to one-third of their body length in just 25 milliseconds, faster than you can blink!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other clubtail species, but the Eastern Least Clubtail is generally smaller than most of its relatives. Remember: if it has a clubbed tail and separated eyes, it's definitely a clubtail — then size and habitat help narrow it down to this species.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name "albistylus" means "white style," referring to pale coloration on part of the male's reproductive structures. Dragonflies are among the most ancient flying insects, with fossils showing their ancestors had wingspans of over two feet during the age of dinosaurs!
compareHints: Since this is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other clubtails in the region. Eastern Least Clubtails are generally smaller and more delicately built than the robust Common Clubtail or the larger Dragonhunter. The separated eyes immediately distinguish all clubtails from the larger darner dragonflies, whose eyes touch at the top of their heads.
